THE CHINA MAIL!
BRITAIN'S PRESTIGE

The "Telegraph" regards the prevalent tendency to excuse the Chinese authorities and minimise personal outrages on British subjects as threatening the prestige of Britain in the War East. The treatment in Canton of two Hongkong journalists is referred to in this connection.

In editorial comment, Mr. Percival Landon's review of the situation in China is regarded as bringing out very clearly the painful fact that the Chinese politicians regard Great Britain and other Powers as their enemies. It is very difficult for British readers to realise this. There is no hostility towards China in England. We are sorry for her; we lament the misery that the collapse of her Central Government has brought upon the oldest of civilised peoples; we are anxious to give her effective help in recovering her ancient peace, though we do not know how to set about it. But of enmity or even dislike there is no trace on our side. Those who concern themselves with Chinese affairs are much readier to blame our Foreign Office for its supposed faults of commission or omission than to denounce the Chinese. It is surely remarkable that the deliberate insult offered to the British Iseigation at Peking by subjecting it to a boycott and constraining the Chinese servants to leave the premises should not have excited public indignation at home, although the Peking Government, in permitting the boycott to continue, has disregarded Treaty stipulations as well as the ordinary diplomatic courtesies. The disgraceful incident at Canton recently, when two British journalists from Hongkong, relying on the Canton Government's assertion that there was no boycott of British shipping, landed on the quay and were immediately seized and thrust into a filthy jail, would have stirred our fathers and grand-fathers to violent wrath. They, in their day, expected British citizens to be treated fairly in every part of the world, and they would have looked for something more than the evasive apology proffered at Canton—an apology not for the unlawful imprisonment, but for the use of the chains in which these unfortunate journalists were led through the city and exposed to the jeers of the mob. But the benevolence with which Great Britain is determined to regard Chinese doings, and the prevalent tendency to excuse the Chinese authorities because all real power is in the hands of military chieftains, may cause even these personal outrages on British subject to be minimised and overlooked, though nothing could be worse for our prestige in the Far East. Yet, in spite of all our resolute manifestations of goodwill towards China, we are reminded by Mr. Landon that the friendliness is all on our side. The Chinese politicians, led by Mr. Wang, who's Moscow's warmest friend at Peking, regard us and the other Powers as enemies, and will enter the coming Conference with the object of doing us harm.
UNPLEASANT FACTS

It is better to face the facts, unpleasant though they are, than to blind ourselves with illusions. China's hostility is bad enough, but the impotence of her self-styled Government is worse from a diplomatic standpoint, because it affords the Powers no hope of remedying her grievances satisfactorily. If President Tuan Chijui and his Cabinet really controlled the Eighteen Provinces the Powers might easily come to terms with him, as Great Britain, America, and Japan are most anxious to restore good relations with their Chinese customers. But the truth is that the President is but the head of a shadow Government, a mere simulacrum of sovereignty, a marionette whose strings are pulled by the inscrutable "Christian" General Feng Yu-hsiang, whose troops occupy the capital, and who receives his munitions by way of Mongolia from his Bolshevik paymasters. Outside Peking and the border Provinces of Shensi and Kansu, which constitute Feng's present zone of occupation, his puppet President is virtually unrecognised, except as the giver of honorific titles to the military leaders who obtain temporary control in the several provinces. The Powers, in negotiating with the nominees of Tuan Chijui, will be dealing with men who have no power to implement their promises, but who undoubtedly will use the Conference as a means of inflaming the anti-foreign movement. As Mr. Tandon points out, the Powers may agree to the proposed increase of the Chinese tariff on

foreign imports, which the Conference has been summoned to discuss. But they will be asked by the Chinese to go further, and to consider the complete abolition of the fiscal treaties and of the extra-territorial rights possessed by foreigners in China. If they refuse to do so the aglators will have fresh material for their propaganda. Yet no discussion of these matters can be helpful while there is no protection for foreigners and their property outside the Treaty ports. Even the tariff question is complicated by the prevailing disorder. As Mr. Landon says, if the Flowers allow the Peking Government to raise some additional millions out of the Maritime Customs they will give fresh offence to all Feng's rivals. He would receive the money, through his obedient servants in Peking, and would spend it in spreading the Soviet agitation. The other Tupans, or Tuchuns, with armies of their own, would want to know why the Powers were thus subsidising Feng against them. We should thus be assisting our bitterest opponent and annoying all the other powerful chiefs. Yet it is difficult to see how the Powers could insist on supervising the expenditure of the new Customs revenue if they agree to its being raised.
CHINA UNITY PROSPECTS.

It may be that some Chinese Napoleon will arise and restore the unity of the Empire. But the recent history of China's civil wars warns us that provincial discussions and the lack of moral sense among the generals make the task of a Chinese Napoleon extremely difficult. Chang Two-lin, the Manchurian ruler, still has what is nominally the largest army, a quarter of a million strong, and exercises control, as far south as Shanghai. His chief rival, Feng Yu-hsiang, who was once the leading commander under Wu Pei-fu, the former over-lord of Central China, and who rose to eminence by betraying Wu in his last struggle with Chang, is now, with Moscow's help, at the head of a force almost as numerous as the Manchurian host, and perhaps as well armed. Whether and when these two potentates, Chang and Feng, who depend respectively on Japan and on Russia, will come into collision no one can say. Nor is it safe to conclude that the victor in the duel, if it came, would necessarily gather Central China, to say nothing of the unruly South, into his fold, and make China one again. Chinese domestic politics are not so simple as that; the fierce animosities existing between the provinces are complicated by party feuds and personal ambitions, so that military victories, real or supposed, have hitherto had no definite results. We may suppose that the anarchy which is wasting China and ruining her trade will come to an end sooner or later, and that force will have to be used to restore order. But to assign a date to this consummation, or to suppose that Chang or Wu, or any other personality now prominent in Western eyes, will achieve the desired end would be very unwise. Our chief hopes must rest on the innate good sense and untiring industry of the Chinese people. If they could somehow be persuaded that the foreigner was not their enemy but anxious to be their friend, and to resume the trade which has benefited all parties engaged in it, they would soon bring about a revival, as they have done many times before in their long history. But how this change of view is to be brought about, in face of the persistent Bolshevik campaign throughout China, is the real problem to which Western diplomats need to address themselves in earnest before still worse mischief has been done.
COAL STRIKE.
Reuter's American Service.)

The country is completely unruffled over the anthracite coal strike which has been proceeding for six weeks. The miners themselves are enjoying a prolonged holiday fishing, camping and touring. Some have taken temporary employment. A number of foreigners are profiting from the opportunity to visit their homes.
The owners similarly are unperturbed. They believe that the strikers will return when their money is spent. In the meantime the country is carrying on with accumulated stocks which however will soon disappear with the approach of winter. The Government hitherto has been reluctant to intervene until the placidity has passed off.

Mr. P. LANDON'S VIEWS.

Mr. Percival Landon, writing from Peking, takes the view that the prospects of the Customs Conference are not of the brightest and that the best hope of achieving some success rests in not shutting our eyes to certain obvious difficulties and dangers which if taken in time may be dealt with although they cannot be avoided.

Before dealing with the many parties. Chinese and foreign, whose interests, amotions, and intrigues are concerned with the Customs Conference in Peking, he writes, it is as well to touch upon certain aspects of the approaching congress which deserve attention at home. Apart from the principles involved there are certain material facts which distinguish this conference from any other and must be understood, if the complexity of the task that lies before the foreign delegates can be understood, or indeed the chance of successful issue estimated Events in China move with such rapidity and their changes are so kaleidoscopic that it may be that a new situation—which means a new military situation—will have arisen before the opening days of November. But however political, financial or military considerations may regroup the forces opposed to the foreign representatives; there will be no change in the consistent anti-foreign complexion of Chinese policy during and probably after the meeting in Peking.

I have used the word “opposed” intentionally, as it would be a grave error to suppose that this conference can be either a friendly adjustment of conflicting interests or is one in which terms are imposed by either side. From the first moment to the last it will be a grim struggle, in which on the one side the interests of foreign States, and, indeed, of China herself, in maintaining and developing trade relations are believed to be vitally concerned, while the other side is blindly convinced that nothing less than Chinese independence is at stake.
A Shadow Government.

The first point to be borne in mind is that the Allies—if the term may be allowed, without indicating in any way an identity of interests—are dealing with a shadow Government that has no power either to conclude a treaty or to enforce any part of it, except by permission of and at the direction of a military autocrat. At the moment it is the Soviet Marshal Feng Yu-hsiang—whose outbreakings of war and slaughter against foreigners will be fresh in the memory of Englishmen—who has the Peking Government under his absolute control. Without his assent from Kalgan or Kansu not a clause will be accepted by the Chinese Government or put afterwards into force.

The second point of practical importance is that the conference will be held in a hostile capital. In itself this characteristic distinguishes this conference from any other international discussion in recent years. In the event of a dissolution of the congress without achieving a satisfactory result, this fact is worth while bearing in mind. To judge by the insults already directed against our own Legation and that of the United States, incidents may occur which may seriously complicate subsequent relations. In respect of these insults, the shadow Government has turned a deaf ear to protests, and a similar attitude on the part of the military autocrat might precipitate grave trouble. Such behaviour as sanctioning the action of those who are terrorising the Legation servants into desertion is inconceivable in any civilised Government, but the fact remains that the Government still tacitly endorses this intimidation, and that consequently the strike continues. It will be in an avowedly anti-foreign atmosphere that this debate will take place. The real enemy will not be directly represented, but every move in China's game will have been suggested or sanctioned from Moscow and played across the council-table by Mr. T. Wang, the ablest of Chinese politicians, and the most thorough adherent of the Soviet Government in China. No doubt he believes that he is merely using Moscow as a tool, but the recent experience of the unhappy Hu Han-min in Canton should teach him that he who sups with the devil needs a loor spoon. But for the moment it is only the avowedly hostile driving force behind the Conference that I wish to emphasize.
Thirdly, it must be remembered that additional revenues from the increase of Customs distractions, to which the Allies are, of course, pledged, will in itself cause acute

dissension in China, even before a treaty is signed. To give it to Peking is tantamount to giving it through Feng, for the spread of Soviet propaganda throughout the Chinese Republic. The other Tupans would only see in the grant a subsidy given by foreign influence to Peking for their undoing. Among these latter Chang Tso-lin himself must be ranked, unless he manages to obtain at least his full share of the increment by a private arrangement with his inevitable enemy Feng. Moreover, we should not overlook the recrudescence of activity from Yochow, whither Wu Pei-fu has been taken himself. On the one hand, nothing is so likely to arouse civil war as the handing over to Peking and Feng Yu-hsiang of any large share of the proceeds of these increased duties; on the other hand, nothing will exacerbate anti-foreign hatred more than any attempt of foreigners to control or deal in any way with this new surplus. It will be useless for foreigners to pretend that, after securing the loans, the use made of the extra revenue is no affair of theirs. The time has gone by when indirect responsibility can be repudiated in China. Certain European nations who used this excuse for pouring arms and ammunition into China during recent years are now regretting their action. If the Conference uses its unquestionable right to assign these extra revenues to Peking—the prisoner of each military autocrat in turn—it cannot plead irresponsibility if the civil war which it has been the constant endeavour of all foreign diplomacy to extinguish blazes up again more savagely than ever.
Powers Must Agree.

In some ways the Peking Conference presents resemblances to that of Lausanne, the course of which may usefully be studied now. Whether actually on the agenda or not, fiscal autonomy and abolition of the Capitulations will figure as, obstinately upon the Peking programme as at Ouchy. The role of Greece as the only possible armed agent of the Allies in an emergency might—and in the event of a civil war inviting the intervention of Russia, must—be played by Japan. Once more the known unwillingness of some Allies, and the inability of others to interfere, will again be a trump card in the hands of our opponent; and we may be certain that any reasonable concessions on our part will be trumpeted through China as proof of our weakness. It is a knot of which Gordius might be proud. For the Allies in Peking to go outside the exact letter of the terms of reference would be sheer folly: yet to refuse to discuss the matters that China is more intent upon than any mere raising of the tariff will infallibly revive the anti-foreign hatred in an acuter form than ever.

The resources of up-agency are great, and it is certain that our action here will vindicate our good faith at Washington; but over this conference there seems to hang the need of a second at a later date, when, to a united China which has proved her capacity to govern without corruption and without injustice, a full measure of independence shall be willingly conceded by the world. Still, it would be a dangerous illusion to cherish the hope that, however generously the Allied delegates may interpret their rights and duties, they will succeed in holding up the present anti-foreign movement which is carrying the red flag of Moscow into every corner of the Chinese Republic.

Last, and perhaps more important than all else, is the necessity of keeping the League of Nations wholly out of this trouble. No conception of the League is more fallacious than that which attributes to it a standpoint based upon universally recognised wisdom, justice, or even expediency. Although its creators were quite unconscious of the fact, neither in concept, on, organisation, nor practice is the League anything but the product of Western civilisation, Western law, and the Western attitudes towards life and even of Christianity. It was, in fact, called together to spread Western ideas, and the presence of such States upon its roll as China or Persia has not availed to broaden its outlook or make its precepts one whit more blastic. There is little in the Chinese outlook upon life which the League would wholly understand; there is even less in the tenets of the League at which in time of stress China would not look askancé. Moreover, in order to preserve the facade of impartiality, the League would draw for its representatives upon precisey those nationality which have no interests in and therefore no knowledge of the East.
